label: Shemu'el Aleph (1 Samuel) — Part 4 — Chapters 25–31
summary_plain: Shemu'el dies. All Yisra'EL mourns. Dawid encounters Naval the fool and Avigayil the wise — she prevents Dawid from shedding blood in anger. Dawid marries Avigayil. Dawid again spares Sha'ul's life — taking his spear and water jug while Sha'ul sleeps. Dawid flees to the Philistines and lives in Tziqlag. Sha'ul, desperate and abandoned by YHWH, consults the medium at Ein-Dor. She raises the spirit of Shemu'el, who declares: YHWH has torn the kingdom from you and given it to Dawid. The Philistines attack at Gilboa. Sha'ul and his three sons — including Yonatan — fall in battle. Sha'ul falls on his own sword.
summary_scholarly: The ACR reads from 4QSam-a and the Orit Ge'ez. 4QSam-a preserves variant readings in the Avigayil narrative and the Ein-Dor account. The death of Sha'ul (ch 31) ends YHWH's experiment with a king chosen by the people's criteria — tall, impressive, from Binyamin. Naval's name means 'fool' — his narrative (ch 25) contrasts human folly with Avigayil's covenant wisdom. The Ein-Dor episode (ch 28) is significant: YHWH has stopped answering Sha'ul through dreams, Urim, or prophets. Sha'ul turns to necromancy — prohibited in Torah — confirming the totality of his rejection. The battle of Gilboa destroys the Saulide dynasty and clears the path for YHWH's chosen — Dawid ben Yishai.

key_terms.definition: The wife of Naval, a wealthy but harsh man who refused to pay David's men for protecting his flocks. When Naval insulted David's messengers, David prepared to kill every male in his household. Avigayil rode out to meet David with provisions, bowed down, and made a covenant speech that stopped the bloodshed. She said: 'The lives of your enemies will YHWH sling away as from the hollow of a sling.' After Naval's death she became David's wife.

His name means 'fool' or 'worthless.' A wealthy man who responded to David's reasonable request for provisions with contempt: 'Who is David? There are many servants nowadays breaking away from their masters.' His refusal was a death warrant for his household. After Avigayil's intervention saved them, YHWH struck Naval and he died within ten days. Avigayil told David: 'YHWH will certainly make my lord a sure house.'

1 Shemu'el 31: the Philistines defeat Yisra'el on Mount Gilboa. Sha'ul's three sons including Yehonatan are killed. Sha'ul is critically wounded by archers and asks his armor-bearer to run him through, but the man refuses. Sha'ul falls on his own sword. The Philistines hang his body and his sons' bodies on the walls of Bet-Shan. The men of Yavesh-Gil'ad travel all night to take the bodies down and bury them.

1 Shemu'el 28: before Gilboa, Sha'ul is terrified and receives no answer from YHWH — no dreams, no Urim, no prophets. He disguises himself and visits a woman who consults the dead at En-Dor. He asks her to bring up Shemu'el. A figure appears; the woman screams when she realizes it is the king. The figure speaks as Shemu'el: 'Why do you consult me? YHWH has become your enemy... tomorrow you and your sons will be with me.'

key_terms.term: David Spares Sha'ul a Second Time
key_terms.definition: 1 Shemu'el 26: David and Avishai find Sha'ul asleep in his camp at night. Avishai urges: 'YHWH has given your enemy into your hand today — let me pin him to the ground with one thrust.' David refuses again: 'Do not destroy him — who can reach out his hand against YHWH's anointed and be guiltless?' He takes Sha'ul's spear and water jug and leaves. The discipline of leaving judgment to YHWH is consistent.

1 Shemu'el 30: while David and his men were away with the Philistine army, the Amalekites raided Ziklag, burned it, and took captive everyone — including David's wives. The men talked of stoning David. 'David strengthened himself in YHWH his Creator.' He asked the priest Evyatar for the ephod, received guidance from YHWH, pursued the Amalekites, and recovered everything.

1 Shemu'el 30:6 — the key phrase when everything had collapsed: Ziklag burned, wives taken, men threatening to stone him. David did not despair. He went to YHWH for guidance before acting. This is the covenant leader's response to catastrophe: not human resourcefulness first, but YHWH consultation first. He then acted decisively on the guidance received — pursuing, defeating, recovering all.

The men of Yavesh-Gil'ad traveled all night to retrieve Sha'ul's body and his sons' bodies from the Philistine walls of Bet-Shan and buried them under the tamarisk tree in Yavesh. They fasted seven days. This act of covenant loyalty preserved Sha'ul's honor in death even after his military failure. David later honored them for it: 'May YHWH show steadfast love and faithfulness to you — YHWH bless you because you showed this loyalty to your lord.'

2 Shemu'el 1 (the opening of the next book) includes David's lament: 'How the mighty have fallen!' He mourns both Sha'ul and Yehonatan. For Yehonatan: 'Your love to me was extraordinary, surpassing the love of women.' He commands it be taught to the children of Yehudah — the lament was to be known and remembered. David's grief for Yehonatan is genuine and covenant-rooted.

In 2 Shemu'el 1, an Amalekite brings David the news of Sha'ul's death and claims he killed Sha'ul at the king's own request. He brings Sha'ul's crown and armlet as proof. David tears his clothes in grief, then executes the man: 'How were you not afraid to reach out your hand to destroy YHWH's anointed?' The man thought bringing David news of his rival's death would earn a reward. He misjudged David's covenant principle entirely.

faq.question: What does Avigayil's speech to David reveal about her character?
faq.answer: Avigayil is one of the most remarkable figures in Shemu'el Aleph. She rides out to meet David independently — without telling Naval — and delivers a speech that is both politically shrewd and genuinely covenant-rooted. She takes responsibility for her household's failure, asks David to spare bloodguilt, and frames her argument in terms of David's future covenant role: 'YHWH will certainly make my lord a sure house' and 'my lord's life shall be bound in the bundle of the living in the care of YHWH.' She sees David's covenant destiny clearly. Her sling-imagery prophecy ('YHWH will sling away your enemies') anticipates David's own weapon of choice against Golyat. She prevents David from an act of vengeance that would have compromised his rule.

faq.question: What does Sha'ul consulting the medium at En-Dor reveal about his spiritual condition?
faq.answer: Sha'ul had himself banished mediums and necromancers from the land — keeping the Torah's prohibition (Devarim 18). Now, in his desperation, he goes to one in disguise. The irony is sharp: he violated his own legal policy. The text says YHWH did not answer him — 'by dreams, by Urim, by prophets.' This total silence is the judgment in action. When YHWH's communication channels are closed, Sha'ul goes to the channel YHWH explicitly prohibited. The figure that appears (whether a genuine apparition or the woman's performance) delivers the same verdict Shemu'el gave in life: YHWH is your enemy, tomorrow you die. Even in Sha'ul's attempt to circumvent the silence, the same word pursues him.

faq.question: Why did David spare Sha'ul a second time when he found him asleep in camp?
faq.answer: The second sparing (ch.26) is not repetition — it confirms David's principle under a different test. The first time (En-Gedi) was an accidental encounter in a cave. The second time, David deliberately enters the camp at night and chooses not to act. Avishai's argument is simpler: 'YHWH has given him into your hand.' David's response is the same principle with added covenant logic: 'YHWH will strike him, or his day will come to die, or he will go down into battle and perish.' David sees three alternatives to killing Sha'ul himself. All three would accomplish the same result without David incurring blood guilt. His repeated refusal is not weakness — it is covenant discipline, the refusal to take shortcuts around YHWH's timing.

faq.question: What covenant significance does the Ziklag crisis carry?
faq.answer: The moment Ziklag burned and David's men talked of stoning him is the bottom point of his fugitive years — his city destroyed, his family taken, his men turning against him. His response — 'David strengthened himself in YHWH his Creator' — is the covenant leader's reflex. He did not strategize first; he sought YHWH first through the ephod. The oracle came back: 'Pursue, for you shall surely overtake and shall surely rescue.' David acted immediately on the word received and recovered everything. The Ziklag pattern is a compressed version of David's whole covenant career: catastrophe → seeking YHWH → receiving direction → decisive action → full restoration. This pattern will repeat in 2 Shemu'el at every major crisis.

faq.question: What made Sha'ul's death on Gilboa a covenant tragedy?
faq.answer: Sha'ul's death was prefigured from 1 Shemu'el 13 — 'your kingdom will not continue.' He knew the verdict for years. His final years were spent pursuing David rather than living into his remaining covenant responsibilities. At Gilboa, the man who had been given every resource for kingship — physical stature, early prophetic anointing, the backing of Shemu'el — died in defeat, abandoned by YHWH, consulting the dead. His sons died with him. The covenant Sha'ul could have established — an obedient covenant monarchy with the Binyamin-Yehudah axis — ended at Gilboa. The tragedy is not that he was rejected but that the rejection was his own doing. He had the capabilities and the calling; what he lacked was the sustained obedience.

faq.question: What does David's lament for Sha'ul and Yehonatan reveal about him?
faq.answer: David composed a formal lament ('The Song of the Bow') and commanded it taught to Yehudah. His grief was not performance — he mourned the man who had tried to kill him. For Sha'ul he grieved the warrior and the anointed: 'How the mighty have fallen!' For Yehonatan his grief was personal and direct: 'Your love to me was extraordinary, surpassing the love of women.' David's covenant heart included the capacity to grieve enemies and love friends without calculating political advantage. The lament was preserved in the Book of Yashar — a covenant document collection that also contained the Sun's standing still from Yehoshua. David's mourning was considered worth preserving alongside the greatest covenant events.

faq.question: What does the Naval episode teach about Avigayil's wisdom?
faq.answer: Avigayil's wisdom is not simply pragmatic intelligence — it is covenant wisdom. She understood the covenant structure David was operating in: he had been anointed, was moving toward his throne, and needed to arrive there without bloodguilt. She intervened not just to save her household but to protect David from himself. Her speech contains genuine covenant prophecy ('YHWH will make my lord a sure house') and genuine covenant appeal (invoking the bundle of the living, the sling metaphor). She reads the moment correctly, acts without her husband's knowledge, and achieves the best outcome for everyone — except Naval, who died by YHWH's hand ten days later, not David's. The covenant structure vindicated itself; she did not need to compromise it.

faq.question: What is the significance of Yavesh-Gil'ad honoring Sha'ul's body?
faq.answer: Yavesh-Gil'ad had a specific covenant bond with Sha'ul: in his first act as king (1 Shemu'el 11), Sha'ul rallied Yisra'el to rescue Yavesh-Gil'ad from Nachash the Ammonite, who had threatened to gouge out the right eye of every man there. They remembered. When everyone else abandoned the dead king, the men of Yavesh-Gil'ad traveled all night — a significant journey — to honor him. David's response when he heard confirms the covenant logic: 'You showed this loyalty to Sha'ul your lord.' Covenant loyalty to those who have served, even after death, is honored by the covenant community. David would later honor Sha'ul's covenant further by protecting Mephiboshet, Yehonatan's son.

faq.question: What does 1 Shemu'el teach about the nature of kingship in the covenant?
faq.answer: The whole of 1 Shemu'el is a thesis about covenant kingship. It opens with YHWH as the true king (Khannah's prayer about YHWH exalting the poor), moves through YHWH's rejection by the demand for a human king, and shows two kings — Sha'ul and David — representing two models. Sha'ul is the king-like-the-nations: impressive appearance, early popularity, military capability — undone by substituting his own judgment for covenant obedience. David is the king-after-YHWH's-heart: flawed, hunted, morally complex — but fundamentally oriented toward YHWH, returning to covenant consultation at every crisis, refusing shortcuts against YHWH's anointed. The book does not idealize David; it shows that covenant fidelity, not human excellence, is the foundation of enduring rule.

faq.question: What connects the Amalekite messenger's death to the broader theme of YHWH's anointed?
faq.answer: The Amalekite thought he was bringing David the news he wanted: his enemy was dead and here was the crown. He may even have fabricated his role in the killing to claim reward. David's response overturned every calculation: mourning, grief, and execution. 'How were you not afraid to reach out your hand to destroy YHWH's anointed?' The anointing was not merely political standing — it was covenant holiness. The man who claimed to have killed the anointed, whatever his motives, bore covenant guilt. David's execution of the messenger is not revenge; it is covenant law: whoever touches YHWH's anointed has committed an act against YHWH. The principle David consistently applied to protect Sha'ul he now applied in judgment against the one who (allegedly) did what David had refused to do.
